extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, graduate students, and writers interested in narratology and narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual distinctions for analyzing or composing narrative mood (how narrative information is delivered), including distance, perspective/focalization, degrees of narration vs. imitation, and types of reported speech. Focuses on how quantity of information and narrator presence produce mimetic or diegetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative mood (overall category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative 'representation' (narrative information) has degrees: the narrative can furnish the reader with more or fewer details, and in a more or less direct way; it can regulate information according to the capacities of knowledge of one or another participant, adopting what we call the participant's 'vision' or 'point of view'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mood is constituted chiefly by two modalities: 'distance' (how directly information is presented) and 'perspective' (which participant's vision is adopted). Treat mood as regulation of narrative information and viewpoint rather than a simple stylistic tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance (diegesis vs. mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of mediation between narrator and story: 'pure narrative' (diegesis) is more distant and mediated, while imitation/mimesis (showing) is less distant and more 'direct'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure distance by how much the narrator intervenes and how condensed or expanded the telling is. Plato's rewrite of Homer illustrates converting direct speech into a more distant, condensed diegesis. Use 'information + informer = C' heuristic: quantity of information and presence of informer are inversely related.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective / point of view (focalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative can choose to regulate information according to the capacities of knowledge of a participant, adopting or seeming to adopt that participant's 'vision' or 'point of view'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which character's consciousness filters events; this focalization affects both what is shown and how 'mimetic' the text feels. Distinguish narrator-as-speaker from narrator-adopting-a-participant's-vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of narrative information
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of narrative detail provided (a more developed or more detailed narrative) is a key factor in producing the illusion of mimesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High quantity of information supports mimesis (showing); low quantity supports diegesis (telling). Quantity is tied to narrative speed (more info → slower speed). Consider both semantic/detail density and temporal exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of the informer (narrator visibility/transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the narrating instance is present or audible in the text — from transparent/absent (narrator unnoticed) to strongly present/mediatizing the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal narrator presence (transparency) helps create the illusion that the story 'tells itself'; strong narrator presence produces mediation and analysis. Evaluate markers of narrator commentary, metanarrative signals, and stylistic intrusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing (Jamesian 'scene' dominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cardinal precept of showing: adopt detailed narrative (scene) and strive for narrator transparency — 'pretending to show is pretending to be silent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically: supply maximal relevant detail while minimizing overt narrator intervention ('dire le plus possible, et ce plus, le dire le moins possible'). Examples: Hemingway's short stories, Flaubertian transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling / diegetic condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensed, mediated narration that reduces events, speech, or inner life to summarized statements (purely narrative/diegesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose telling by looking for condensed statements that transform speech or event into brief reports ('I decided to marry Albertine'). Recognize it's not 'worse' per se but produces distance and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative speed (tempo) related to information quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of information is in inverse ratio to narrative speed: more information typically slows the narrative; less information speeds it up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing pacing, relate perceived speed to level of detail and to degree of narrator mediation. Use this to explain why 'scene' slows time while summary speeds it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative of events vs. narrative of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between narrating nonverbal events (always a verbal transcription, hence only an illusion of mimesis) and narrating words (which can be closer to literal reproduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect narrative of words to allow stronger imitation (quotation, repetition), while narrative of events always involves representation; assess whether 'mimesis' claims are plausible depending on which is being narrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of contingent/useless detail as referential illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Useless or contingent details (e.g., 'the loud-sounding sea') function as connotators of mimesis by giving the narrative a sense of 'reality' and referential richness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot details that serve no plot function but create a 'referential illusion' — their presence often signals an attempt to mimic reality and to produce mimetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and reader variability of mimetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived mimetic quality of a text depends on historical period, audience sensitivity, and individual readers; the same passage may be more mimetic to one reader or era than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating 'showing' vs 'telling', situate the text historically and consider readership conventions — what seemed mimetic in one era may appear merely descriptive or prolix in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratized (narrated) speech
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three states of character speech: narratized (narrated) speech is the most distant and most reduced (e.g., 'I informed my mother of my decision'), often close to pure event-reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this category to diagnose a high degree of narrator mediation; expect minimal fidelity to original utterance and strong summarizing language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposed speech (indirect style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect or transposed speech reports a character's words or thoughts through the narrator's syntax ('I told my mother that I absolutely had to marry Albertine'), more mimetic than narratized speech but still clearly mediated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for subordinate clauses and explicit reporting verbs; transposed speech can be extended but retains the narrator's linguistic imprint and does not guarantee literal fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free indirect style
rubrics_metrics.description: A variant where economizing on subordination allows greater extension of character speech while merging narrator and character voice; absence of a declarative introductory verb often creates ambiguity between character thought and narrator commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect free indirect style by syntactic shifts (no reporting verb) and subtle merging of voices. Note its double confusions: between uttered vs inner speech and between character vs narrator voice. It provides partial emancipation of character speech without full obliteration of the narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate speech / interior monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech where the narrator is obliterated and the character's speech/thoughts are presented directly (e.g., interior monologue), often beginning 'from the first lines' and operating without narrative patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify by first-person present-tense unfolding of thought as if without an auditor. This is the most 'mimetic' form because the character substitutes entirely for the narrator; examples include Joyce's interior monologue and sections of Ulysses and The Sound and the Fury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported (direct) speech as dramatic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotation of characters' utterances (dramatic dialogue or monologue) — adopted since Homer as the basic form of dialogue, producing a high degree of mimesis in the Platonic/Aristotelian sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify quotation marks, vocative markers, and dialogic formatting. Reported speech is classically the mimetic ideal for reproducing characters' words and can operate alongside other modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradations and blends of speech modes
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, the idealized forms (narratized, transposed, free indirect, immediate) blend and slide imperceptibly in texts; narrators often move between modes to produce subtle effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid categorization when analyzing texts: trace shifts and transitions among modes (e.g., narrated → indirect → free indirect) and observe how these shifts serve characterization, pacing, or thematic emphasis. Use examples (Proust passages) to map such movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox of simultaneous showing and telling
rubrics_metrics.description: A single narrative can combine extreme showing (rich scenes) and extreme telling (strong narrator presence) simultaneously, creating a paradoxical effect (as in Proust: intense detail yet constant narrator mediation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating narrative technique, note cases where rich mimetic detail coexists with explicit narrator commentary; interpret this as a deliberate normative transgression rather than an error, and analyze its rhetorical/affective aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of speech to event as narratizing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators can reduce spoken words to events (e.g., 'Agamemnon refused and dismissed Chryses'), turning discourse into action and thus increasing diegetic distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this tactic as a means of achieving narratized speech; it's useful for summarization, quickening tempo, or asserting narrator control. Assess its impact on character presence and on the reader's sense of authenticity.
